name: Provide in-centre hemodialysis
summary: People whose kidneys have failed come to the hospital's dialysis unit three times a week for treatments of about four hours, on a fixed chair and shift. A hemodialysis nurse, usually caring for three patients at once, sets up the machine, assesses the patient, puts two needles into the fistula or connects the central catheter, runs and watches the treatment, gives medications and monthly blood work, and ends the run; an assistant then cleans the station for the next patient, and nephrologists review patients on weekly rounds. Late patient transport, low blood pressure on the machine, access problems and machine faults push back the whole shift.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation running about 40 in-centre hemodialysis stations on three patient shifts a day, six days a week, with a home dialysis program.
baseline.notes: Unit of work is one in-centre hemodialysis session, from the patient's arrival to leaving the unit. Home dialysis, vascular access surgery and nephrology clinic visits are separate processes.

trigger: A patient on the unit's standing schedule arrives for a booked chair and shift under a nephrologist's dialysis prescription.
end_state: The treatment is complete and documented, the patient has left the unit and the station is cleaned for the next shift; or the patient was sent to the emergency department or missed the session.

volume.seasonality: Steady; patients dialyse three times a week all year. Holiday weeks shift sessions to other days, and winter storms cause late arrivals and missed sessions.

evidence.note: 37,964 dialysis visits in 2021/22 (3,164 a month) and 37,171 in 2020/21 (3,098 a month). The published count may include some home-program clinic visits, so in-centre sessions could be slightly lower.

One nurse to three patients (blake2020, lhsc_renal) over about 5 hours of chair time per session gives about 1.7 nurse hours per session, about 5,300 hours a month or 40 to 42 FTE; the 70 headcount includes part-time nurses and the home program.
Technologists maintain machines and the water treatment system; per session they only respond to machine faults, so most of their time is not counted in this process.

Canadian units increasingly give non-clinical tasks to lower-paid staff (blake2020); 15 minutes of station cleaning per session is about 6 FTE. Cost estimated on the organisation file's 1.35 loading of a patient care assistant wage.

roles.title: Consultant specialist (internal medicine, cardiology, nephrology, oncology and others)

evidence.note: Nephrologists round weekly on each dialysis patient and are on call for problems.
A patient care manager runs the dialysis units (schedules, chair allocation, incidents).

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Pharmacy information system and automated dispensing cabinets
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
Ontario Renal Reporting System (provincial renal data portal)

steps.name: Arrive, wash the access arm and weigh in
steps.description: The patient arrives by car, taxi, accessible transit or patient transport, washes the fistula arm, steps on the unit scale, and waits in the waiting room until the station from the previous shift has been cleaned.

evidence.note: Arrival routine from general knowledge of Ontario dialysis units; late and missed shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Set up and prime the dialysis machine
steps.description: The nurse checks the station's machine passed its self-test and disinfection, hangs the dialyser and blood lines, primes them with saline and sets the dialysate bath to the patient's prescription. Often this is done while the patient is weighing in.

error.defect_description: Wrong dialysate bath or dialyser for the prescription.

control.basis: Pre-treatment machine safety check (alarm, conductivity and disinfectant-residual tests)

evidence.note: Machine set-up including priming took about 2 to 4 minutes of operator time in a time-motion study (grundler2021); the range here adds fetching supplies and checks. Nurses rather than technicians set up in many Ontario units (author's knowledge).

steps.name: Assess the patient before treatment
steps.description: The nurse compares the weight with the target dry weight to set the fluid removal goal, takes blood pressure, pulse and temperature, asks about symptoms since the last run, screens for infection, and looks, listens and feels the access for a thrill or signs of infection.

error.defect_description: Fluid removal goal miscalculated (wrong dry weight or weight entered).

evidence.note: Pre-dialysis assessment is routine; the catheter share (about 45%) reflects high catheter use in Canadian units and is the author's estimate. The queue is the nurse starting three patients at the same time.

steps.name: Cannulate the fistula or graft
steps.description: The nurse cleans the skin, inserts the arterial and venous needles using the patient's usual sites or buttonholes, tapes them, and checks flow with a saline flush. A missed or infiltrated needle needs another attempt, often by a more senior nurse.

control.basis: Vascular access cannulation protocol and infection prevention (skin antisepsis)

evidence.note: Needling is done by nurses in Canada; non-nurse needling is rare (blake2020). Times and the miss rate are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Connect the central venous catheter
steps.description: Wearing mask and sterile gloves, the nurse removes the caps, scrubs the hubs, withdraws the lock solution, checks both lumens flush and draw, and connects the lines; poor flow is reversed or treated.

error.defect_description: Break in aseptic technique (catheter infection risk).

control.basis: Central line access protocol (aseptic technique) per IPAC best practice

evidence.note: Catheter connection under aseptic technique from general knowledge of dialysis nursing; times estimated.

steps.name: Start the run and program the prescription
steps.description: The nurse connects the blood lines, starts the blood pump, gives the heparin dose, and programs treatment time, blood flow, fluid removal and dialysate settings, then checks pressures and that every alarm is armed before documenting the start.

error.defect_description: Programmed time or fluid removal does not match the prescription.

evidence.note: Treatments of 3 to 4 hours prescribed from measured urea clearance, three times a week (blake2020); monthly blood work is about 1 session in 13. Medication share estimated.

steps.name: Draw and send the monthly blood work
steps.description: On the unit's monthly blood-work day the nurse draws pre-dialysis samples from the access before heparin and post-dialysis urea afterwards, labels them from the standing order in the laboratory system and sends them to the laboratory.

error.defect_description: Mislabelled tube or post-dialysis sample drawn at the wrong time.

control.basis: Two-identifier specimen labelling at the bedside

evidence.note: Monthly blood work drawn by dialysis nurses from the access is standard practice; the organisation file instead routes a lab order to specimen collection.

steps.name: Give IV medications on the machine
steps.description: The nurse checks the electronic medication record and gives the scheduled intravenous medications into the blood line: the erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, iron and vitamin D analogue doses set by the anaemia and bone protocols, recording each in the eMAR.

error.defect_description: Dose omitted or given twice in the week.

evidence.note: Protocol-driven anaemia and mineral medications are given on the machine in most units; frequency estimated.

steps.name: Monitor the patient and machine during the run
steps.description: Through the treatment the nurse checks blood pressure and pulse about every 30 to 60 minutes, watches arterial and venous pressures and the fluid removal rate, answers alarms, checks needle sites stay visible and taped, and charts each check while watching two other patients.

error.defect_description: Falling blood pressure or a needle dislodgement noticed late.

control.basis: Venous needle dislodgement precautions: access site kept visible, venous pressure alarm limits

evidence.note: Total nursing care of about 59 minutes per treatment (kleijn2015) at one nurse to three patients (blake2020); the monitoring share is the author's split.

steps.name: Review the patient on nephrology rounds
steps.description: On the patient's weekly rounds day the nephrologist reviews the run sheets, weights, blood pressures and the monthly blood results with the nurse, examines the patient at the chair and adjusts the dry weight, prescription and medications.

control.basis: Dialysis prescription and medication orders signed by the nephrologist

evidence.note: Weekly nephrologist rounds during treatment are typical of Ontario hospital units; time per patient estimated. Rounds overlap the treatment, so no wait is counted.

steps.name: Treat low blood pressure or cramps
steps.description: The nurse lays the patient flat, slows or stops fluid removal, gives a saline bolus, rechecks blood pressure, and calls the nephrologist if it does not recover; the run may be shortened.

evidence.note: Intradialytic hypotension is the most common complication; frequency of about 10% to 15% of sessions is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Replace a faulty machine
steps.description: When a machine alarms repeatedly or fails a check, the nurse returns the patient's blood if possible and calls the dialysis technologist, who swaps in a spare machine, primes it with the nurse and tags the faulty one for repair in the maintenance system.

evidence.note: Machine faults in about 2% of sessions and repair handling are the author's estimates.

steps.name: End the treatment and remove the needles
steps.description: When the prescribed time is up the nurse returns the blood to the patient with saline, removes the needles and holds pressure until bleeding stops (or flushes and locks the catheter with the prescribed lock solution and caps it).

evidence.note: The wait is the remainder of the 3 to 4 hour prescribed treatment (blake2020) after the start and monitoring steps; the patient is being treated, not queued.

steps.name: Assess after treatment and document
steps.description: The nurse weighs the patient, takes standing and sitting blood pressure, checks the access sites have stopped bleeding, and completes the treatment record (fluid removed, blood volume processed, problems) in the hospital information system.

error.defect_description: Treatment record incomplete or weight not recorded.

evidence.note: Post-dialysis assessment and documentation are routine; times estimated.

steps.name: Strip and disinfect the station
steps.description: After the patient leaves the chair the unit assistant removes and discards the lines and dialyser, wipes the machine, chair, table and scale with disinfectant, starts the machine's heat or chemical disinfection cycle and sets up clean linen for the next shift.

control.basis: Infection prevention and control routine practices: clean and disinfect the station between patients

evidence.note: Between-patient cleaning per IPAC routine practices; 10 to 20 minutes per station is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the ride home
steps.description: The patient waits in the lounge for family, taxi or accessible transit; rides booked for a fixed time often arrive late or early, and patients who feel faint stay longer under observation.

evidence.note: Transport waits estimated from general knowledge.

steps.name: Arrive late because of transport or weather
steps.description: A storm, a late transit pickup or traffic makes the patient arrive late; the shift then starts late, or the treatment is shortened so the next shift can start on time.

evidence.note: Winter storms and transit delays are a known cause of late and missed dialysis in Ontario; frequency estimated.

steps.name: Follow up a missed session
steps.description: When a patient does not arrive, the nurse phones the patient and family, checks for illness or hospital admission, offers a make-up session on another shift if a chair is free, tells the nephrologist, and records the missed treatment.

evidence.note: Missed-session follow-up from general knowledge; share of about 2% estimated.

steps.name: Send an unwell patient to the emergency department
steps.description: If the patient has chest pain, shortness of breath from fluid overload, a fever with a catheter, or a very high potassium, the nurse calls the nephrologist and arranges transfer to the emergency department with a written report; urgent dialysis then happens as an inpatient.

evidence.note: About 1% of sessions; author's estimate.

steps.name: Restore catheter flow
steps.description: For a catheter that will not draw, the nurse repositions the patient, flushes and reverses the lines, and if the nephrologist orders it instils a clot-dissolving lock and tries again, documenting the dysfunction for the access team.

next.condition: flow restored or run with reversed lines

evidence.note: Catheter dysfunction management from general knowledge; share estimated.

steps.name: Enter monthly data in the provincial renal system
steps.description: Once a month per patient the nurse or unit clerk updates the patient's dialysis modality, access type and treatment counts in the Ontario Renal Reporting System from the unit's records.

error.defect_description: Access type or modality change not updated.

control.basis: Ontario Renal Network funding and reporting requirements for dialysis programs

evidence.note: Monthly patient-level reporting to the Ontario Renal Network is the author's knowledge; the system name is from general knowledge and was not checked.

exceptions.name: Intradialytic hypotension
exceptions.description: Blood pressure falls during the run; fluid removal is stopped and saline given, and the run may be shortened.

exceptions.name: Late arrival
exceptions.description: Weather or transport delays the patient; the treatment starts late or is shortened.

exceptions.name: Missed session
exceptions.description: The patient does not come; the nurse follows up and offers a make-up session.

exceptions.name: Access problem
exceptions.description: A needle infiltrates or a catheter will not flow, delaying the start.

exceptions.name: Machine fault
exceptions.description: A machine fails during the run and the technologist swaps it.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from arrival to leaving the unit

evidence.note: Treatments last 3 to 4 hours (blake2020); the author adds about 45 to 75 minutes for weighing in, set-up, assessment, ending and the ride home, giving about 5 to 5.5 hours door to door; p50 and p90 are the author's derivation.
SD 24.30 minutes.

benchmarks.unit: nurses per patient on the machine

evidence.note: 1:3 is now common (blake2020) and is the LHSC in-centre ratio (lhsc_renal).

pain_points.description: Patients on one shift all start within the same half hour, so each nurse sets up, assesses and needles three patients back to back and starts run late.

evidence.note: Author's knowledge of fixed-shift dialysis unit flow.

pain_points.description: Late transport, storms and long between-shift cleaning push each shift later, leading to shortened treatments or evening overtime.

evidence.note: Units run fixed staff shifts from about 07:30 to 23:00 (lhsc_renal), so delays accumulate into the last shift; delay causes are the author's knowledge.

pain_points.description: High central catheter use brings poor flow, extra aseptic steps and infection risk.

evidence.note: Author's knowledge of Canadian vascular access patterns.

pain_points.description: Treatment data are kept in the hospital record and re-entered monthly in the provincial renal system and unit spreadsheets.

evidence.note: Author's knowledge.

sources.supports: Canadian in-centre hemodialysis units are staffed by registered nurses; staffing ratios of one nurse to three patients are now common (one to two was frequent earlier); typical treatment lasts 3-4 hours driven by measured urea clearance; centre units typically run three shifts a day and most patients dialyse three times a week; non-clinical tasks are increasingly given to lower-paid staff but needling by non-nurses is rare.

sources.supports: Observational study of 242 patients in 12 Dutch centres: average nursing care time for four routine domains was 59.23 minutes (SD 24.30) per treatment per patient.

sources.title: Less Complexity in Hemodialysis Machines Reduces Time and Physical Load for Operator Actions (U. Gruendler, E. Ekesbo, M. Loewe, A. Gauly), Medical Devices: Evidence and Research 14:379-387
sources.supports: Time-motion study: machine set-up including priming took 3.70 minutes on a Fresenius 5008 CorDiax and 1.94 minutes on a 6008 CareSystem; the newer machine cut total operator time per treatment by about 2.6 to 2.8 minutes.

assumptions: Describes the common practice of an Ontario hospital in-centre hemodialysis unit in 2019-2022, not Halton Healthcare's own procedures.

Station cleaning is done by a dialysis unit assistant (added as dialysis_assistant, not in the organisation file). If nurses or the 8 technologists did it instead, the technologist headcount would not cover 15 minutes for 3,130 sessions a month (about 6 FTE at 130 productive hours).
The trigger is the standing dialysis prescription from the nephrology clinic, as in the organisation file; each session is in practice started by the standing schedule.

Monthly blood work is drawn by dialysis nurses from the access and sent directly to the laboratory (dx-lab-testing, lab_specimen), not as a lab order to specimen collection as the organisation file has it. The workflow also adds outputs to the ED (unwell patients), pharmacy (medication orders), biomedical equipment (faulty machines) and environmental cleaning.
The provincial renal data system (orrs) is added as a system; its name is from general knowledge and was not checked against an Ontario Renal Network page.

Dialysis nurse FTE (42) is set by the 1:3 ratio over about five hours of chair time per session; the simulated hands-on minutes (about 70 nurse minutes per session) imply fewer FTE because nurses also supervise their other patients between tasks.

40 stations on three shifts a day, six days a week give about 3,120 session slots a month, so the unit runs close to full; the station is held for about 4.5 hours per session including set-up and cleaning.
Shares (catheter 44%, late 5%, missed 2%, hypotension 12%, machine fault 2%, sent to ED 1%) are tier C estimates.
